definition: A reason or purpose for designing and executing a test. Typical test objectives include evaluating work products, finding defects, gaining confidence, preventing defects, and providing information for decision-making.
An aspect of the test basis that is relevant to achieve specific test objectives. A test condition can be a component, function, feature, behavior, or any identifiable element that can be tested.

A set of input values, execution preconditions, expected results, and execution postconditions, developed to cover test conditions such as a path through a component or system, a specific function, or a particular state.
A sequence of test cases in execution order, and any associated actions that may be required to set up the initial preconditions and any wrap-up activities post execution.
A collection of test cases or test procedures that are grouped together for a specific testing purpose, such as regression testing, smoke testing, or acceptance testing.
The process of running a test on the test object, producing actual results, and comparing these actual results to the expected results. Test execution can be manual or automated.
An imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications. A defect is introduced by a human (error) and can cause a failure when executed.
A human action that produces an incorrect result. An error (mistake) made by a developer, tester, or other team member can introduce a defect (bug) into a work product.
The state of a software product or component containing a defect that may cause a failure when the code is executed under certain conditions. Often used synonymously with defect.

An event in which a component or system does not perform a required function within specified limits, producing an incorrect or unexpected result. A failure is the observable consequence of a defect being executed.
The percentage of specified coverage items that have been exercised by a test case or a set of test cases. Coverage items can be requirements, code statements, branches, paths, or data conditions.

A black-box test design technique in which input data is divided into partitions of equivalent data from which test cases can be derived. Values in each partition are expected to be processed in the same way by the test object.

A black-box test design technique in which test cases are designed based on the boundary values of equivalence partitions. It focuses on values at the edges of partitions where defects are most likely to occur.

A black-box test design technique that uses a table showing combinations of inputs and/or stimuli (conditions) with their associated outputs and/or actions (consequences) to design test cases. Useful for testing business logic with multiple conditions.

A black-box test design technique in which test cases are designed to execute valid and invalid state transitions. The system is modeled as a finite number of states, with transitions triggered by events or conditions.

A white-box test design technique measuring the percentage of executable statements in the source code that have been exercised by a test suite. 100% statement coverage means every line of code has been executed at least once.

A white-box test design technique measuring the percentage of decision outcomes (e.g., true/false branches of if-statements) that have been exercised by a test suite. Stronger than statement coverage as it tests decision logic.

An experience-based test technique where the tester uses their knowledge of past defects, application behavior, and common failure modes to anticipate where defects are most likely to occur and design tests specifically for those areas.

An experience-based test technique in which testers simultaneously design and execute tests, using their domain knowledge, analytical skills, and creativity to discover unexpected defects. Test execution and learning happen in parallel.

A static test technique in which a work product or a set of work products is examined by one or more individuals to find defects, suggest improvements, assess quality, or build consensus. Reviews can be informal or formal.

A type of formal review with a defined process, roles, and entry/exit criteria. Inspections are led by a trained moderator and follow a structured approach to find defects in work products. The most rigorous type of review.

A type of review in which the author of a work product leads reviewers through the document to gather feedback, achieve consensus, and increase confidence. Less formal than technical reviews and inspections.
The ability to identify related items in documentation and software, such as requirements, test cases, defects, and test results. Traceability helps assess coverage, impact analysis, and compliance.
Artifacts produced during the test process, such as test plans, test design specifications, test cases, test procedures, test data, and test reports. Testware is a subset of software work products.

A source of information that can be used to determine whether the actual results of a test execution match the expected results. Examples include specifications, user manuals, reference systems, or domain knowledge.
Data that exists before a test is run and that affects or is affected by the component or system under test. Test data may be created specifically for testing or taken from production environments.

An environment containing hardware, instrumentation, simulators, software tools, and other support elements needed to conduct a test. The test environment must be controlled and representative of the production environment.

A specific instantiation of a test process against a particular level of the software development lifecycle. Common test levels include component testing, integration testing, system testing, and acceptance testing.

A group of test activities based on specific test objectives and targeting specific characteristics of the test object. Examples include functional testing, non-functional testing, white-box testing, and change-related testing.

Testing performed after a defect has been fixed to verify that the original defect has been successfully removed. Also known as re-testing. Confirms that the fix works as intended for the specific defect scenario.

Testing performed to detect unintended side-effects of changes in a component or system. Regression testing re-runs existing tests to ensure that previously working functionality still works after modifications.
Testing performed on a deployed system to evaluate its ability to continue to function correctly after modifications, migrations, or retirement. Includes impact analysis to scope the testing effort.

A potential event or condition that could have a negative impact on a project, product, or organization. In testing, risks are categorized as product risks (related to product quality) or project risks (related to project management).

The degree to which a component, system, or process meets specified requirements, user needs, and expectations. Testing contributes to quality by finding defects, assessing conformance, and providing information about the level of quality.

Confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled. Verification answers the question 'Are we building the product right?' and often involves static testing techniques.

Confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled. Validation answers the question 'Are we building the right product?' and often involves dynamic testing.

The process of finding, analyzing, and removing the cause of a failure in a component or system. Debugging is performed by developers, not testers. Testing identifies failures; debugging identifies and fixes the underlying defects.

The fundamental reason for the occurrence of a problem or defect. Root cause analysis identifies underlying process or system deficiencies so that corrective actions can prevent recurrence of similar defects.

The use of software tools to control the execution of tests, compare actual outcomes to predicted outcomes, set up test preconditions, and report test results. Automation increases efficiency for repetitive tests but requires maintenance effort.

A document describing the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of intended test activities. It identifies test items, features to be tested, testing tasks, personnel, risks, and contingency plans.

Conditions that must be met before a defined set of test activities can begin. Entry criteria help ensure that the test object and test environment are ready for testing, reducing waste and false defect reports.

Conditions that must be met to conclude a defined set of test activities. Exit criteria define when testing is sufficient and can include coverage targets, defect density thresholds, or residual risk levels.

Testing performed without executing the code of a component or system. Static testing examines work products such as requirements, design documents, and code through reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, and tool-based analysis.
Testing that involves the execution of the software of a component or system. Dynamic testing evaluates the behavior of the software in runtime and compares actual results against expected results.

A software product that supports one or more test activities, such as planning, design, execution, data management, reporting, and defect tracking. Tools can increase efficiency but require investment in selection, training, and maintenance.

A test level that focuses on individual components or units of software in isolation. Typically performed by developers using white-box techniques, with access to the code and often using unit testing frameworks.

A test level that focuses on the interactions between components or systems. Integration testing can be performed at different levels (component integration, system integration) and aims to find interface defects.

A test level that focuses on the behavior and capabilities of a complete system or product. It validates end-to-end functionality and evaluates non-functional characteristics such as performance, security, and usability.

A test level that focuses on determining whether a system satisfies its acceptance criteria and whether the customer or user will accept the system. Includes user acceptance testing (UAT), operational acceptance testing, and regulatory acceptance testing.

A type of testing that evaluates the functions that a component or system should perform. Functional tests verify that the software behaves according to specified functional requirements, using black-box techniques.

A type of testing that evaluates characteristics of a component or system that are not related to specific functions or user actions. Includes performance, reliability, usability, security, portability, and maintainability testing.

The body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and test design. The test basis can include requirements, specifications, use cases, user stories, design documents, risk analysis results, and domain knowledge.

A risk directly related to the quality of a software product, such as potential defects, performance issues, security vulnerabilities, or usability problems. Product risks can lead to failures in production and impact user satisfaction.

A risk related to the management and execution of a project, such as resource shortages, unrealistic schedules, budget overruns, organizational changes, or political issues. Project risks can affect the project's ability to deliver.

The systematic process of identifying, analyzing, prioritizing, and mitigating risks throughout the project lifecycle. In testing, risk management helps focus effort on the most critical areas of the system.

A high-level description of the test levels to be performed and the testing within those levels for an organization or program. The test strategy is derived from business requirements and risk assessments.

The process of checking the status of test activities, identifying any variances from planned activities, and reporting progress to stakeholders. Test monitoring uses metrics such as test case execution rate, defect discovery rate, and coverage achieved.

The process of taking corrective actions based on test monitoring information. Test control decisions may include reprioritizing tests, adjusting test schedules, reallocating resources, or changing the test approach.

The process of recognizing, investigating, taking action, and disposing of defects throughout the testing lifecycle. It involves logging defects, tracking their status, prioritizing fixes, and verifying resolutions.

A discipline applying technical and administrative direction and surveillance to identify and document the functional and physical characteristics of a configuration item, control changes, and record and report change processing and implementation status.

The final phase of the test process where test artifacts are archived, lessons learned are documented, and the testing effort is formally concluded. Test completion ensures knowledge retention for future projects.

termFr: Cycle de vie du développement logiciel
definition: Software Development Life Cycle. A framework defining tasks performed at each step of the software development process. Testing activities are integrated into the SDLC and vary depending on the chosen model (waterfall, iterative, agile).
